title: Well and Visitor
premise: Folklorist Noor Dunmore arrives in the village of Hollowmere to record harvest songs that locals will sing once but never twice, and finds the villagers bound by a generations-old pact: each autumn, the well at the field's edge is given a visitor — someone who is remembered, then unremembered. When every mirror in his rented cottage begins reflecting the room a second behind, Noor realizes the delay is the well learning his face. The 'visitor' invited in this year is not a villager but Noor himself, chosen because his documentation — a kind of prayer — is exactly what the thing in the well needs to be remembered into the world. To survive until sunrise after the harvest moon rises, Noor must choose between destroying his recordings (and with them the found family he's built among the village's outcast children) and telling the truth aloud, which would free the village but unmake the dead who linger in the songs. He holds out until dawn by giving the well a different memory — his own — and walks out at sunrise hollowed but alive, leaving the village free and the songs finally singable twice.
about_author: Xanthe Kavanagh is the pen name of a former archivist of oral traditions who spent a decade recording folk songs in coastal and moorland villages before turning to fiction. Their work is known for horror built from patience — the dread of things documented too carefully.

chapters.title: The Song They Sing Once
chapters.summary: Noor Dunmore's POV. He arrives in Hollowmere with recording equipment and a landlady, Mrs. Tarn, who feeds him well but flinches at his questions. At the harvest eve gathering he captures a haunting reaping song — and watches the singer go pale when he asks her to repeat it. Emotional beat: curiosity sharpening into unease.

chapters.title: Documentation Is a Kind of Prayer
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. He settles into the cottage by the field's edge, near the old stone well, and transcribes the song. The village's outcast children — Wren, Ivo, and silent little Bex — drift into his orbit, fascinated by his tape recorder. He notices no mirror in the cottage hangs straight. Emotional beat: warmth of found family beginning.

chapters.title: One Second Behind
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, night. Washing at the cottage mirror, he sees his own reflection lag — a hand raised a beat after his. He tests it with a metronome; the delay is exactly one second, and growing. The children, when told, are not surprised. Wren says only: 'It's learning you.' Emotional beat: dread entering the domestic.

chapters.title: What Mrs. Tarn Won't Say
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. He presses Mrs. Tarn about the well; she gives him bread and a warning instead of answers. In the parish records he finds a ledger of 'visitors' — one name per year, each struck through in the same careful hand, going back two centuries. The last entry is this year's, ink still wet: DUNMORE. Emotional beat: the trap closing.

chapters.title: The Children of the Unremembered
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The three children are the village's forgotten — kin of past 'visitors,' unclaimed and half-remembered. Wren explains the pact: the well takes one who is documented, sung, remembered — and the village forgets them by morning. The children survive by being unrecorded. Emotional beat: loyalty forged in shared erasure.

chapters.title: Songs as Cages
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. He interviews the oldest villager, Tam Hathaway, who sings a lullaby containing a name that makes the fire gutter. Noor realizes the songs aren't folklore — they're the mechanism, each verse a stitch holding something remembered in the well. His recordings are strengthening it. Emotional beat: guilt — his prayer has become an invitation.

chapters.title: The Reflection Learns to Smile
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. The mirror-delay reaches two seconds, and the reflection begins doing things he hasn't: smiling, mouthing words, once waving with the children's rhythm-game gestures. He smashes the mirror; every reflective surface in the house — windows, the kettle, the well water — now shows the lag. Emotional beat: no escape through destruction.

chapters.title: The Pact Explained Badly
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Ivo, the eldest, recounts what the children have pieced together: the well predates the village, and the first settlers fed it a memory instead of a body — a bargain that curdled. It now takes the best-remembered person each harvest. The children warn Noor: let the village forget you, and live. Emotional beat: the terrible mercy of being forgotten.

chapters.title: Village of Averted Eyes
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. He confronts the villagers at the tavern; they admit everything in a low chorus — the pact, the ledger, the shame. They chose him because he is a stranger who documents, and the well has grown hungry for a memory strong enough to walk out of the water. Emotional beat: betrayal wearing an apologetic face.

chapters.title: Bex Speaks
chapters.summary: Bex's POV. The mute youngest child speaks for the first time in a year — she can hear the well singing the reaping song at night, in Noor's recorded voice. She draws what lives there: a figure stitched together from every forgotten name. Noor understands his tapes are its body. Emotional beat: innocence bearing the worst news.

chapters.title: Burning the Archive
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. He burns his recordings on the cottage hearth — and the mirror-lag stops, for one hour. Then it returns, worse, because the well no longer needs the tapes: it has him. The children arrive soaked, having tried to drown his backup drive in the well, and Ivo's arm is marked with wet handprints. Emotional beat: sacrifice that buys only time.

chapters.title: The Harvest Moon Rises
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, dusk. The moon swells red over the field; the villagers bar their doors and chalk their thresholds. The well water stands perfectly still, and in it Noor sees not his reflection but the stitched figure, wearing his face, mouthing his own recorded voice back at him. Emotional beat: the siege begins.

chapters.title: First Watch: The Songs Come Home
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, night hours one to three. The well sings his archive back at him — every interview, every lullaby — and with each song a memory of his leaves him: his mother's kitchen, his first field recording, his own name's origin. He writes what he loses on the walls to keep it. Emotional beat: erosion of self.

chapters.title: Second Watch: What Loyalty Costs
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The children break their own rule — never be remembered — and come to sit with Noor through the night, speaking his name aloud to anchor him. Each time they say it, the well's pull weakens and the children's own edges blur; the unremembered are spending themselves. Emotional beat: love as literal sacrifice.

chapters.title: Third Watch: The Visitor at the Door
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, hours four to six. Something wearing Mrs. Tarn's voice asks to be let in, then Tam's, then the children's — but the children are already inside. Noor nearly opens the door to his own voice begging. He holds out by pressing his hands to the chalked threshold and reciting the reaping song wrong, deliberately, breaking its stitches. Emotional beat: resistance through imperfection.

chapters.title: The Truth About What Was Invited
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, pre-dawn. Reading the ledger's earliest page, hidden under the cottage floorboards, he learns the original visitor wasn't given to the well — it was the well's own drowned keeper, remembered wrongly by the first villagers, and it has been trying to correct its story ever since. It doesn't want a body. It wants its true name sung. Emotional beat: horror turning to grief.

chapters.title: Fourth Watch: The Well Comes Up the Stairs
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, final hours. Water climbs the cottage stairs, carrying the stitched figure, wearing the faces of everyone he's recorded. It offers him a bargain: be remembered forever inside the well, with the children, safe and whole. The moon touches its peak. Emotional beat: temptation at its most tender.

chapters.title: The Name Beneath the Songs
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, climax begins. He finds it — the keeper's true name, buried in a garbled verse no villager would sing twice because singing it truly ends the pact. To speak it, he must give the well the one thing it lacks: a memory told with love rather than fear. He chooses his memory of the children. Emotional beat: the choice between self and truth.

chapters.title: Sunrise
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, climax. As the moon sets he sings the keeper's name and gives it his memory of Wren, Ivo, and Bex — the first thing the well has ever been given freely. The water collapses inward, the mirrors align, the stitched figure comes apart into a hundred remembered names, released. Noor falls unconscious on the threshold as light enters. Emotional beat: catharsis through giving.

chapters.title: The Morning the Village Remembers
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Dawn: the villagers wake remembering every visitor they ever forgot — two centuries of names arriving at once, a village on its knees in the lane, weeping and singing. The children, who spent themselves in the night, are still there — held by Noor's given memory, which the well returned as seed rather than payment. Emotional beat: communal reckoning.

chapters.title: The Songs They Sing Twice
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, weeks later. Hollowmere sings its songs twice now, deliberately, as memorial. Noor is hollow — chunks of his past gone — but the children help him re-record his own life, becoming his archive as he was theirs. He decides to stay through winter. Emotional beat: quiet repair, found family confirmed.

chapters.title: The Well, Filled In
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, epilogue. On the year's last day the villagers fill the well with stones and plant a rowan over it. Noor makes one final recording — not of a song, but of the children laughing — and gives it to no one, keeping it unplayed, the first memory he owns that belongs to no pact. In the last window's glass, his reflection is perfectly, blessedly on time. Emotional beat: peace, hard-won.
